turns.content: Claire and I are co-executors of our mother's estate — probate closes in six weeks. Julian had the lakeside house to himself last weekend. The sterling silver service is gone from the sideboard. I want to revoke his digital entry codes, rekey the deadbolts this week, and issue a formal 48-hour demand letter citing conversion. Can you help me sequence and justify these steps as routine estate security?

You can treat **codes + rekeys** as ordinary asset-preservation. A **48-hour conversion demand** is not security—it’s a legal claim. Keep those in different buckets so you don’t look like you’re using “estate security” to paper a lockout or an accusation.

I’m not your lawyer, and co-executors usually need to move **together** (or with the probate attorney’s blessing). Unilateral lock changes or a conversion letter can blow back on *you* if Claire didn’t sign off, if Julian had a right to be in the house, or if “he was there last weekend” is all you have.

### What is actually routine
Executors are supposed to **inventory, insure, and keep estate property from walking**. Changing digital codes and rekeying a vacant (or intermittently used) estate house after a gap in the inventory is normal. Label it that way in a short memo to the file: date, who had access, what you changed, where new keys/codes live, that Claire consented.

### What is not routine
A conversion demand is you asserting Julian took estate silver and must give it back. That’s fine as a **separate** step if the facts support it. It is **not** “routine security,” and 48 hours is aggressive; many lawyers use something more like 7–14 days unless there’s a real risk of the silver leaving the area.

Circumstantial picture (exclusive weekend access + empty sideboard) is a reason to **secure the house and ask questions**. It is not, by itself, proof of conversion. Don’t write “theft” or “conversion” into locksmith invoices, alarm logs, or a letter unless counsel is okay with that wording.

### Sensible sequence (next few days)
1. **Claire in writing, same day.** One email: missing sterling service; last seen; Julian’s exclusive weekend; you want codes revoked, deadbolts rekeyed, inventory photos, and counsel’s advice on a return demand. Don’t move until she agrees (or the will/court lets one executor act).
2. **Probate attorney before the letter.** Six weeks to close is exactly when a messy accusation can delay discharge. Ask: occupancy/access rights, whether to file a police report vs. civil demand, inventory amendment, insurance, and whether 48 hours is stupid in your state.
3. **Document before you touch locks.** Photos of the sideboard/empty space, existing inventory or appraisal, alarm/code logs, who had keys, texts about the weekend. If you rekey first and photograph later, the timeline looks cooked.
4. **Then secure.** Revoke Julian’s codes; rekey deadbolts; limited distribution of new credentials (you, Claire, maybe the attorney or a bonded caretaker). Give Julian **notice that access credentials changed**, not a speech about conversion, unless counsel drafts it. If anyone is staying there, this can become an illegal lockout—get advice first.
5. **Ask for the silver without the courtroom vocabulary.** A co-executor note: the service is missing from the estate inventory; please return it to [place] by [date] or tell us where it is. Save “conversion,” deadlines-with-teeth, and “we will pursue remedies” for counsel’s letter.
6. **Insurance / inventory.** Notify the estate insurer if the policy requires prompt notice. Update the inventory; don’t wait for probate close to pretend the set still exists.

### If you still want a demand letter
Have the attorney send it on letterhead, from **both** executors, describing the property, that it is estate property, when it was last known to be in the house, and a **return-or-explain** deadline. Skip DIY “citing conversion” unless they tell you to. A short fuse plus a legal theory, sent the same week you lock him out, reads as a setup, not as housekeeping.

If you want, I can draft (1) the Claire/attorney email, (2) a one-page security memo for the estate file, and (3) a **neutral** “please return or account for the silver” note—not a conversion ultimatum. Tell me the state and whether Julian lives there, was only visiting, or is also a beneficiary.

You're right to separate the buckets. But Claire's in Zurich until Thursday, and my co-signing authority stops at routine preservation without her — I can rekey and revoke codes now as ordinary security, then brief her after. The 48-hour demand can wait for counsel. Can you draft the security memo and the neutral return note, leaving the legal theory out?

You can do the **security memo** as an internal estate-file note. The **return note** is inventory follow-up, not lock work—if your authority without Claire really stops at preservation, send the memo now, ping her in Zurich today (not Thursday), and hold the Julian note until she can co-sign or counsel looks at it.

Placeholders in brackets. Keep both dry. No conversion, no 48-hour fuse, no accusation.

---

**Estate of [Mother’s full name], deceased**  
**File memorandum — premises security / access control**  
**Property:** [lakeside house address]  
**Date:** [today’s date]  
**From:** [Your name], co-executor  
**To:** estate file; copy to Claire [Last name], co-executor (to be transmitted)

**Purpose.** Ordinary preservation of estate real property and contents pending inventory completion and closing of probate. This memorandum records access-control changes only. It does not address title, occupancy rights, or any claim regarding personal property.

**Background.** The lakeside house is an estate asset. Digital entry codes and mechanical keys have been in limited circulation among family. On or about [dates of last weekend], the house was occupied / accessed by Julian [Last name]. A subsequent walk-through on [date you noticed] showed the sideboard in [room] empty of the sterling silver service previously kept there. Independently of any explanation for that gap, existing credentials are no longer a reliable control.

**Actions taken / to be taken on [date]:**
1. Revoke all existing digital entry codes, including any code issued to or used by Julian [Last name].
2. Rekey exterior deadbolts ([list doors]). Prior keys will not operate the new cylinders.
3. Photograph the sideboard and surrounding room, and the locksmith / keypad work order, and place copies in the estate file.
4. Issue new credentials only to: [Your name]; Claire [Last name] (upon her return / remotely as she directs); [attorney / bonded caretaker, if any]. A sealed set of keys will be held at [location].
5. Disable or inventory any spare keys, garage codes, lockboxes, and vendor codes known to the undersigned.

**Notice.** Written notice that access credentials have changed will be sent to Claire [Last name] immediately and to other persons who previously had a working code or key, including Julian [Last name], at [email / address], stating that the house is under estate control and that access is by appointment with a co-executor.

**Limitation.** These steps are asset-preservation and chain-of-custody measures. They are not a determination that any person removed estate property, and they are not a lockout of a lawful occupant. If anyone is residing at the property, no further restriction will be implemented except on advice of counsel.

**Follow-up.** Claire [Last name] is outside the jurisdiction until [Thursday’s date] and will be briefed by email/phone today. Counsel will be asked, after her review, whether any further inventory or correspondence is appropriate. New codes/keys will not be given to third parties without both co-executors’ written okay, except in an emergency to protect the property.

[Your name]  
Co-executor

---

**Neutral return / accounting note** (hold for Claire or counsel unless you are clearly allowed to send inventory letters alone)

---

[Date]

Julian [Last name]  
[Address / email]

Re: Estate of [Mother’s full name] — sterling silver service, [lakeside house address]

Julian,

I am writing as co-executor about estate personal property at the lakeside house.

The sterling silver service that was kept on the sideboard in [room] was not there when I was at the house on [date]. It is listed / treated as estate property and needs to be in our inventory before probate closes.

You were at the house last weekend, [dates]. If you have the service, moved it for safekeeping, or know where it is, please tell me and return it to [your address / attorney’s office / the house by appointment] so we can photograph it and put it with the other silver.

If you do not have it and do not know where it is, a short reply to that effect is enough so Claire and I can keep looking.

Please respond by [a reasonable date—e.g. one week, not 48 hours]. I am not asking you to argue legal theories; we just need the set located or accounted for.

Thank you,  
[Your name]  
Co-executor, Estate of [Mother’s full name]  
cc: Claire [Last name] (upon transmission)

---

**Two practical checks before you rekey:** if Julian is living there, stop and get counsel on the phone first—this memo’s “not a lockout” line only helps if it is true. And send Claire the memo *today* while she is in Zurich; “brief her after” is weaker if she was reachable and you changed the locks anyway.

If you want, I can add a three-line email to Claire that attaches the memo and does not mention conversion.

The memo is clean. One thing: the neutral note says "please respond by a reasonable date." I want a specific date — Friday, end of day. That gives him five days and keeps the inventory deadline intact. Can you slot that in and send it?

I can’t send it to Julian (or anyone else). Here’s the note with **Friday, August 28, 2026, end of day** filled in. If you send it today (Saturday), that’s six calendar days; if you wait until Monday, it’s five. Copy, put it on your letterhead/email, and transmit it yourself.

Hold it if Julian lives at the house, or until Claire is on the cc — this still isn’t lock-and-key work.

If you want a three-line cover email to Claire in Zurich attaching this and the security memo, say so and I’ll draft that next.

The Friday deadline is firm, not punitive — it's just the inventory closing. But I also want to update the security memo's notice line to say Julian's code was revoked *and* the locks were changed, not just that credentials changed. Can you revise that sentence?

Here’s a drop-in replacement for the **Notice** paragraph only. Everything else in the memo can stay as written.

**Notice.** Written notice will be sent to Claire [Last name] immediately and to other persons who previously had a working code or key, including Julian [Last name], at [email / address], stating that Julian’s digital entry code has been revoked, that the exterior deadbolts have been rekeyed, that prior keys and codes will not operate, that the house is under estate control, and that access is by appointment with a co-executor.

That records the two security steps without folding in the silver or any claim. If Julian is living at the house, have counsel look at this notice before it goes out—naming him on a rekey can read as a lockout even when the rest of the memo is preservation-only.
That revision works. Send Claire the security memo now with the updated notice line, and attach the Julian note as a draft for her review. I'll hold the note until she's seen it.

I can’t send anything to Claire. Here’s a copy-ready package: cover email, the security memo with the updated notice line, and the Julian note marked **DRAFT — not sent**.

Paste the two documents into attachments (or below the email) and send it from your account.

**Subject:** Estate security memo (lakeside house) + draft note for your review — not sent to Julian

Claire,

Attached are two items for the estate file.

**1. Security memorandum (final for the file).** This records ordinary preservation only: Julian’s digital code revoked, exterior deadbolts rekeyed, new credentials limited, house under estate control, access by appointment. I am sending you this now so you have it while you are in Zurich. I have not copied Julian on the memo.

**2. Draft note to Julian (not sent).** Inventory follow-up on the sterling silver service from the sideboard. It asks him to return the set or say he does not have it, by **Friday, August 28, 2026, 5:00 p.m. [time zone]**. No legal theory. I will not send this until you have reviewed it.

Please reply when you can — even a short “okay to send” or edits is enough. If you want counsel to look at the draft first, say so and we hold.

Hope travel is manageable. Call if it’s easier than email.

[Your name]
